drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: Here is your opening item. An insurer's claims intake runs the same three steps for every claim
drills.answer_line: SAM: That is the core of it. The answer is A, a workflow.
drills.stem: Every claim runs the same three steps: extract fields, check the policy record, route to an adjuster queue. An autonomous agent sometimes routes before checking the policy, and cost and latency are over budget. What is the best change?

options.A: Rebuild as a workflow: three calls in a fixed sequence in code, with a programmatic check between steps
options.B: Add a line in capitals to the system prompt: policy check always before routing
options.C: Move to a larger model that follows instructions more reliably
options.D: Split into a supervisor agent with three subagents, one per step

drills.why: Same steps every claim means a known path: put the order in code where it cannot be skipped. B is a polite instruction, C makes skips rarer not impossible, D adds 3-10x tokens and leaves order to a model.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A bank's research team wants an assistant
drills.answer_line: SAM: B. "Nobody can say in advance" is the agent tell
drills.stem: Analysts' questions vary: some need one filing, others a dozen filings, news searches and a pricing lookup, and nobody can say in advance which sources a question needs. What is the best architecture?

options.A: A fixed three-step chain: search, summarise, answer
options.B: An agent with search and lookup tools in a loop, with stopping conditions such as a turn limit
options.C: A routing workflow sending each question to one of four fixed pipelines
options.D: A single call with every recent filing pasted into the context

drills.why: Unpredictable steps are the agent tell; stopping conditions bound the loop. A and C fix the path; D pastes data instead of giving access.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. A support platform team is deciding where subagents
drills.answer_line: SAM: A is right. C is the role split we just named
drills.stem: Choose two. Which two situations justify a subagent?

options.A: A diagnosis step reads thousands of log lines, but the main agent needs only the probable cause
options.B: Three independent account-history questions that can be investigated at the same time
options.C: Writing a code fix and its unit tests, split into a coder agent and a tester agent
options.D: A simple FAQ assistant with four tools and short answers
options.E: Outlining, drafting and polishing one reply, each by its own agent

drills.why: A is context protection, B is parallel independent work. C and E split one context by role or phase (telephone game); D has nothing to solve.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. For each statement, say custom loop, Agent S D K, or Managed Agents.
drills.answer_line: SAM: Three out of four. Four is Managed Agents with a self-hosted sandbox.
drills.prompt: Custom loop, Agent SDK, or Managed Agents? 1) Own tool dispatch, own retries, control of every step. 2) Claude Code's file and shell tools, compaction and subagents, on your own Kubernetes. 3) Three-person team, long-running sessions, no hosting or sandboxes to run. 4) Anthropic runs the loop, but generated code executes in your cloud.
drills.answer: 1) Custom loop. 2) Agent SDK. 3) Managed Agents. 4) Managed Agents with a self-hosted sandbox.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A field-service company's operations agent
drills.answer_line: SAM: A. It stops the call before it executes, deterministically.
drills.stem: An Agent SDK operations agent must never run a destructive command against the production database, whatever a ticket says. What should the developer implement?

options.A: A PreToolUse hook on the shell tool that inspects each command and denies destructive ones against production
options.B: A system prompt section, in capitals, listing forbidden commands
options.C: A PostToolUse hook that pages on-call whenever a destructive command has run
options.D: A larger model less likely to follow malicious ticket text

drills.why: "Must never" needs a deterministic control before the call. B is guidance, C is detective, D is a bigger model.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. A healthcare provider's documentation agent
drills.answer_line: SAM: Both. A answers the rule lost in compaction
drills.stem: Choose two. After hours, an Agent SDK agent stops following a formatting rule from the first prompt, and each morning's session spends an hour re-reading records to see what yesterday finished. Which two changes address the causes?

options.A: Move the rule into the project CLAUDE.md the SDK loads, re-injected on every request
options.B: Give the agent the memory tool and a progress log read at session start and updated before the end
options.C: Turn compaction off so nothing is summarised
options.D: Raise the maximum number of turns
options.E: Use the largest context window and paste yesterday's full transcript each morning

drills.why: A survives compaction; B carries state between sessions. C lets the window fill, D fixes a cap neither symptom touches, E is context rot on purpose.

drills.question_line: SAM: Recall first. Pause and name the five segments, and the giveaway that points to each.
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Workflow or agent; subagents; building the agent
drills.prompt: Name the five segments, and the giveaway that points to each.
drills.answer: Workflow or agent; subagents; building the agent; hooks; memory and context. Same or unpredictable steps; verbose or independent work; who runs the loop; must never; forgets or drifts.

In this episode: Workflow or agent, from the stem's wording
When a supervisor with subagents pays for itself
Own loop, Claude Agent SDK, or Managed Agents
Hooks for actions that must or must never happen
Keeping a long-running agent's context clean
Cold open: the claims pipeline: Domain 1: Agents and Workflows, 14.7%, about 8 items
Answer style: purpose-built mechanism for the stated constraint
Segment one: workflow or agent: Workflow: model and tools on predefined code paths
Agent: the model directs its own process and tool use
Simplest first: single call, then workflow, then agent
Agents cost more and their errors compound
Overnight, cost-first bulk job: the Batch API
Segment two: supervisors and subagents: Supervisor decomposes, delegates with scoped tools, combines
Default: start with a single agent
Multi-agent: about 3-10x the tokens of one agent
Split by context, not by role
Good boundaries: independent paths, clean contracts, blackbox checks
Segment three: building the agent: Own loop: tool_use block, run tool, tool_result, repeat
Agent SDK: Claude Code's harness as a library, in your process
Built-in tools, compaction, subagents, sessions, hooks
Managed Agents: Anthropic runs the harness and sessions
Axis: who runs the loop, and where tools execute
Loop controls: max turns, max budget
Segment four: hooks for deterministic ac: Hooks: your code at fixed points in the agent loop
Run in your process, cost no context
PreToolUse: allow, deny, ask, or rewrite input
PostToolUse: audit, add context, side effects
Matchers match tool names; check paths inside the hook
Segment five: loops, memory, context and: Context accumulates across turns; context rot
A bigger window postpones the limit, not the rot
Subagents isolate; context editing clears old tool results
Compaction summarises older history near the limit
Start with the API; understand what a framework sends
Cold open: the verdict: Answer: A, a workflow with the order in code
Supervisor plus subagents: more tokens, order still model-chosen
Capitals in the prompt: guidance, not a guarantee
Bigger model: rarer skips, not none
Five to remember: Workflow: predefined paths; agent: self-directed, with stopping conditions
One agent first; subagents for context, parallel work, specialisation
Own loop for control; Agent SDK on your infra; Managed Agents hosted
Must always or never: a hook; matchers match tool names
Manage context: isolate, clear, compact, CLAUDE.md, memory tool
Recap: the exam tells: Sources unknown in advance → agent with turn limit or budget
Session flooded or paths independent → subagent
Planner, coder, tester on one job → telephone game, keep one agent
Full loop control → own loop; your servers → Agent SDK; no infra → Managed Agents
Must never → PreToolUse hook; after-the-fact alert is detective
Early rule forgotten → CLAUDE.md; fresh start each session → memory tool
Framework hides prompts → look underneath it
